title: Why does Spring recommend putting @Transactional on the concrete implementation class rather than on the interface?
shortTitle: @Transactional on interface vs implementation — CGLIB proxy pitfall

s1_definition.profdef: JDK dynamic proxies (interface-based) honor interface annotations. CGLIB proxies (class-based, Spring Boot DEFAULT) may silently IGNORE annotations on the interface. Placing `@Transactional` on the implementation is ALWAYS safe regardless of proxy type. Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default (`spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true`), so annotate the IMPLEMENTATION.
s1_definition.oneliner: JDK proxy reads interface annotations, CGLIB (Spring Boot default) reads class annotations. Annotate the IMPLEMENTATION class — it works for both proxy types.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** JDK dynamic proxies (interface-based) honor interface annotations. CGLIB proxies (class-based, Spring Boot DEFAULT) may silently IGNORE annotations on the interface. Placing `@Transactional` on the implementation is ALWAYS safe regardless of proxy type. Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default (`spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true`), so annotate the IMPLEMENTATION.

**One line to remember:** JDK proxy reads interface annotations, CGLIB (Spring Boot default) reads class annotations. Annotate the IMPLEMENTATION class — it works for both proxy types.

sections.s2_technical:
Spring creates a proxy around every `@Transactional` bean. There are two proxy styles. A JDK dynamic proxy implements the bean's interface and can read `@Transactional` from the interface method. A CGLIB proxy creates a runtime subclass of the concrete class and reads `@Transactional` from the class. Spring Boot sets `spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true` by default, so CGLIB is used even when interfaces exist. That is why an annotation sitting only on the interface can be silently ignored.

When the annotation is on the implementation, both proxy styles see it. For example, placing it on the concrete method is always safe: `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) public void transfer(...)`. The AOP metadata resolver (`AnnotationTransactionAttributeSource`) scans the target class first, so the implementation annotation always wins. A senior-level nuance: if you later switch to interface-based proxies for a specific bean, implementation annotations still work, but interface-only annotations break — so implementation placement is the portable, future-proof choice.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India refactored its transfer code to depend on a `TransferService` interface for testability. A developer moved `@Transactional` onto the interface method, assuming Spring would honor it. Because Spring Boot uses CGLIB proxies by default, the annotation on the interface was never seen. Rajesh's debit from SAV2001 and Priya's credit to CUR3001 ran WITHOUT a transaction — a crash after the debit left money missing.

This is exactly the interface-versus-implementation proxy pitfall. The fix is to annotate `TransferServiceImpl` instead of the interface. The code below shows the broken version, the corrected version, and the recommended class-level pattern on the implementation.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer request of Rs.50,000 from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001), served by a bean behind a CGLIB proxy.

**Step 1.** The controller calls `transferService.transfer(...)`. The injected reference is actually the CGLIB proxy subclass of `TransferServiceImpl`, not the raw object.

**Step 2.** The proxy inspects the TARGET CLASS `TransferServiceImpl` for `@Transactional`. Because the annotation is on the implementation method, the proxy finds it and begins a transaction (connection checked out, auto-commit disabled).

**Step 3.** Inside the transaction the real method debits SAV2001 (1,000,000 to 950,000) and credits CUR3001 (250,000 to 300,000). Both use the same thread-bound connection.

**Step 4.** The method returns normally, so the proxy commits. Had the annotation been on the interface only, the proxy would have found NOTHING on the class, run the method with no transaction, and a mid-method crash would have left the debit un-rolled-back.

**Step 5.** The connection returns to the pool. Both balances are now durably updated.

```
INFO  [http-nio-8225-exec-1] TransferServiceImpl - TX active (annotation on impl) debit SAV2001 Rs.50000
INFO  [http-nio-8225-exec-1] TransferServiceImpl - credit CUR3001 Rs.50000
INFO  [http-nio-8225-exec-1] TransferServiceImpl - COMMIT ok: SAV2001=950000, CUR3001=300000
```

```
  Proxy implements interface → reads annotations from interface → works ✅
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Interface vs Implementation Annotation (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Proxy Pattern:   CGLIB subclass wraps TransferServiceImpl        │
  │     WHY: adds transaction behavior without changing business code │
  │  Strategy/DI:     Controller depends on TransferService interface │
  │     WHY: Dependency Inversion — swap impls, mock in tests         │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: TransferServiceImpl only does transfers                       │
  │  O: new transfer rule = new impl, interface unchanged             │
  │  D: Controller → TransferService (interface), not the concrete    │

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │     <<interface>>             │
  │     TransferService           │        (NO @Transactional here)
  │  ──────────────────────────── │
  │  + transfer(from,to,amt): void│
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ implements
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │   TransferServiceImpl         │  @Transactional on THIS class/method
  │  ──────────────────────────── │
  │  - accountRepo: AccountRepo   │  ◇ aggregation
  │  ──────────────────────────── │
  │  + transfer(from,to,amt): void│  throws InsufficientFundsException
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ wrapped by (subclass)
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │ TransferServiceImpl$$CGLIB    │  ← Spring-generated proxy
  │  + transfer() { begin; super; │
  │      commit/rollback; }       │
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. Controller.transfer("SAV2001","CUR3001",50000)
  2.   → CGLIB proxy.transfer(...)        reads @Transactional on IMPL ✓
  3.     → txManager.getTransaction()     BEGIN
  4.     → TransferServiceImpl.transfer() real method
  5.       → accountRepo.debit("SAV2001")
  6.       → accountRepo.credit("CUR3001")
  7.     → txManager.commit()             COMMIT
  8.   → return (balances durable)

  Contract for transfer():
    Pre:  from/to exist, from.balance >= amount
    Post: from debited, to credited, atomically (both or neither)
    Fails if annotation on interface only under CGLIB → NO TX → not atomic
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
For multiple DataSources, each needs its own PlatformTransactionManager selected by name in the Transactional annotation. A single Transactional cannot atomically span two databases without JTA/XA. In microservices, use Saga plus Outbox for cross-service consistency instead of distributed transactions.

TransactionSynchronization callbacks let you register afterCommit logic within the transaction method — an alternative to TransactionalEventListener for one-off callbacks. readOnly equals true optimizes reads by skipping Hibernate dirty checking and hinting the JDBC driver to route to a read replica. TransactionalEventListener with AFTER_COMMIT is the safest way to trigger external side effects. The BEFORE_COMMIT phase allows last-minute work that participates in the transaction.

The Modifying annotation on Query UPDATE/DELETE queries tells Spring Data it is a DML statement. clearAutomatically clears the persistence context after the bulk update so subsequent reads get fresh data. Always put Transactional on the implementation class, not the interface — Spring Boot uses CGLIB proxies by default which may not see interface annotations. The implementation annotation works regardless of proxy type.
